appraisal_events.evidence: ils hébergeaient — avec la parfaite innocence d’honnêtes hôteliers qui ont chez eux, sans le savoir, un célèbre brigand — un des membres les plus élégants du Jockey-Club, ami préféré du comte de Paris et du prince de Galles, un des hommes les plus choyés de la haute société du faubourg Saint-Germain ; and the Aristée / Ali-Baba similes for the hidden splendour of his other life.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator decisively elevates Swann by disclosing that the familiar neighbour the family classifies as a stockbroker’s son is in fact at the summit of aristocratic society, and by figuring his concealed life as a mythic kingdom or a cavern of unsuspected treasures. The whole apparatus of the family’s caste thinking is set up only to be overturned by this revelation.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Êtes-vous seulement connaisseur ? [...] vous devez vous faire repasser des croûtes par les marchands » ; « On peut dire que vous êtes un vrai type, monsieur Swann ! » ; « Eh bien ! M. Swann, vous habitez toujours près de l’Entrepôt des vins [...] ? » Et elle regardait du coin de l’œil, par-dessus son lorgnon, les autres visiteurs ; « Oui, chez une princesse du demi-monde ! »
appraisal_events.explanation: The great-aunt systematically withholds recognition from Swann — denying him competence in the one field he cares about, staging him before visitors as an amusing eccentric, and reducing his real high-society evening to a joke about a demi-mondaine. The narrator ironizes the performance by naming her the one slightly vulgar member of the family and by having already told the reader what she cannot see.

status_effects.explanation: Swann’s standing rises sharply in the passage: he is revealed as a Jockey-Club figure and intimate of the comte de Paris and the prince de Galles, immeasurably above the caste position his hosts assign him.
Inside the household frame Swann is patronized: credited with no expertise, cast as a comic turn for the family’s visitors, and obliged to absorb the great-aunt’s jibes in silence.
Her mockery recoils on her: the narrator marks her as the only slightly vulgar person in the family, and the reader already knows her serene irony is aimed at a man whose world she cannot imagine.

ambiguities: The text itself leaves the great-aunt’s laughter undecidable — « sans qu’elle distinguât bien si c’était à cause du rôle ridicule que s’y donnait toujours Swann ou de l’esprit qu’il mettait à les conter » — so « vous êtes un vrai type » can be read either as belittling or as unwitting tribute to Swann’s wit; this affects how sharply negative E2 is toward Swann.

The final two paragraphs slide from « ma grand’mère » to « ma tante » without renaming the speaker. Read here as the grand’tante (same lorgnon, same public irony, same Paris jibes), but the surface form could be taken for another aunt, which would change the source attribution of the closing snub.
